content: Perinatal infections in neonates are predominantly bacterial in origin. These infections can be acquired either from the mother before or during birth or from environmental sources after delivery. Premature infants are particularly susceptible to perinatal infections due to their underdeveloped immune systems. Neonates, especially those born prematurely, have a very limited ability to exhibit symptoms, which means even subtle deviations from normal behavior should raise suspicion for bacterial disease. Chronic congenital and perinatal infections are often asymptomatic in both the mother and the neonate. These infections may remain latent or sub-clinically active within the host tissues for extended periods. Over time, they can cause insidious damage to the central nervous system and sensory systems. When these infections become clinically apparent, they almost always result in mental or sensory impairments, or both. Cytomegalovirus is the most common cause of congenital infections, and primary maternal infection during pregnancy can have devastating effects on the fetus. Perinatal infections that occur within the first few days to 14 days of life are typically caused by pathogens present in the cervico-vaginal canal during delivery. Common causative organisms include Escherichia coli, Group B beta-hemolytic streptococci, Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonococci), Listeria monocytogenes, Bacteroides species, Candida albicans, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus type 2. The morbidity and mortality associated with both acute and chronic perinatal infections are significant, necessitating prompt and aggressive diagnosis and treatment. Late-onset perinatal infections, which typically occur between 3 to 6 weeks after birth, are caused by environmental pathogens. Common causative organisms include Klebsiella species, Aerobacter, Proteus species, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Coxsackie B virus, Candida albicans, echovirus, influenza virus, parainfluenza virus, and respiratory syncytial virus. Several vertically transmitted infections are grouped under the TORCH complex, which includes: T: Toxoplasmosis caused by Toxoplasma gondii. O: Other infections (detailed below). R: Rubella. C: Cytomegalovirus. H: Herpes simplex virus type 2 or neonatal herpes simplex. The other infections category includes: Parvovirus B19. Coxsackievirus. Chickenpox caused by varicella-zoster virus. Chlamydia infection. HIV. Human T-lymphotropic virus. Syphilis. Zika fever caused by the Zika virus, which can result in microcephaly and other brain abnormalities in the child. Hepatitis B.
